newsitem.title: EGYPT: Interest in Egyptian minerals picks up after lull.
newsitem.headline: Interest in Egyptian minerals picks up after lull.

text.p: Eight foreign mining companies, encouraged by improvements in Egypt's investment climate, are negotiating for prospecting concessions, the head of the Egyptian Geological Survey and Mining Projects said on Tuesday.
"There is a very big rush these days, probably because of the current favourable atmosphere," Gaber Naeim told Reuters in an interview.
The level of interest compares with a total of six agreements signed between the mid-1980s and the early 1990s with foreign companies, only one of which remains active in the ground.
Naeim said that previously, Egypt demanded very high royalties, something that drove away potential investors.
In the best known case, the British firm Minex spent $4.5 million in four years on gold prospecting but later withdrew because the level of royalties was so high, he said.

"The first agreement was tough (on the foreign company) because it was made similar to the oil agreements of the time," he said. The state took 80 percent of production, with only 20 percent going to the foreign partner.

"This gave investors a very bad impression of us. Whenever an investor came in, he asked us what happened with Minex," said Naeim. It took the country six years to win back the confidence of investors, he added.
Things have changed, especially since Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri took office early last year with a mandate to accelerate the pace of economic liberalisation.

Foreign capital has since flooded into the Egyptian stock exchange and money markets, especially after the Middle East economic conference in Cairo last November. Standard and Poor's gave the country an investment-grade rating early this year.
"The recovery (of foreign interest in mining) started at the beginning of the 1990s... (but) about 50 percent of the current negotiations started after the economic conference," Naeim said.
Naeim said that in the current negotiations the government's share of production might range around the three to seven percent level, a far cry from the 80 percent in the Minex case.

He declined to name the eight companies negotiating but said that six of them -- three Canadian, one Saudi-Canadian, one UAE-Canadian and one South African -- were negotiating on prospecting for gold in the Eastern Desert and southern Sinai.
An Indian firm is in negotiations on quarrying Sinai sand, among the finest in the world, while a Spanish company is trying to quarry stone such as marble and granite in the peninsula.
The only foreign mining company now operating in the country is Pharaoh Gold Mines of Australia, which is looking for gold in the Eastern Desert and plans to start production in mid-year.
"Mining in Egypt has a good future," Youssef el-Rajhi, general manager of the Pharaoh branch in Egypt, told Reuters. "The Eastern desert has a large potential."
